pillar_reactions.evidence: Delivered with the progression argument and aimed at his endurance goals — 'we're getting the strength. It's directly helping the endurance things' — plus a promise about the shoulders. The prospect volunteered his own supporting anecdote unprompted, which is the strongest engagement signal on the call: 'that halo movement. I saw that on maybe his page and I was like, what the hell does that do? That looks stupid. Like did it a handful of times. was like, man, this is awesome. Like, yeah, I can really feel it in my shoulders without having to do all the stupid other shoulder stuff I've been doing.' He also confirmed the mobility ask directly: 'I know I need to do more mobility specifically.'

Pitched at the fluctuation problem he had already named — 'we just want to cut out that fluctuation. That's the main thing that we want to do with this' — and at travel. He agreed without elaboration: 'sounds like it's, uh, hits what I'm, uh, looking to do', and immediately turned it into a commercial question: 'Is it a, you mentioned six months, is it a six month minimum or how's that work?' Later he confirmed nutrition was one of the two things that actually mattered to him — 'I don't want to do the strength piece without the nutrition piece' — which makes the flat in-the-moment reaction worth noting: the pillar he cared most about drew the least response.

Delivered fully, including direct text access to Trevor, form review, weekly check-ins and the teach-to-fish exit. The prospect's entire response was 'Nope' to questions and 'Sweet'. No enthusiasm and no pushback. Notable given that he had explicitly named accountability on the diet as one of his two must-haves — 'just could use some accountability on the diet piece' — and had also said he does not want face-to-face contact: 'I don't care about, like, you know, face-to-face calls. If it's asynchronous, it's really good.' The pillar was pitched as high-touch to a prospect who had asked for low-touch.

anchors.raw: the options I'm weighing is, like, going to that Future app and comparing, just like, you know, what's $199? Can be from Future, do they have somebody that could, you know, program some kettlebell workouts?
anchors.competitor: Future (app-based remote coaching, approximately $199 per month)
anchors.note: A named, priced, human-coached competitor at roughly a fifth of the monthly equivalent, and he stated on the way out that comparison shopping was exactly what he would do next: 'I will probably just get on Instagram and just like, find some price comparisons.' The rep did engage it — arguing that an app gives a workout programme rather than customisation, nutrition or skill transfer — which is the right argument, but it came after the price had already been cut twice, so it read as justification rather than positioning.

anchors.raw: I was thinking like 250 a month was the maximum that I was ready to pull the trigger on right now.
anchors.note: The hardest ceiling in the batch and it was in place before the call — 'I was just going to go with the first option that was within my price range.' $6,000 over six months is four times it, and he did the arithmetic out loud twice. Crucially the ceiling was never tested: not one financial-picture question was asked, so whether $250 was a real constraint or an expectation was never established. The manager's read afterwards was that it was an expectation problem, not a capacity one, which makes the unasked questions more costly.

anchors.raw: I mean, it makes sense given that like, I mean, I didn't even realize that he had, you know, over a million followers until I looked him up just now, uh, on Instagram. So like literally, literally just now, as we were talking… I mean, like, you know, probably running the model of, uh, whenever you're at capacity, double price. It's awesome that he's able to do that, uh, and charge so much for it.
anchors.note: The prospect built the price justification himself, mid-call, having Googled the founder while the number was being quoted. He arrived at premium-pricing-by-demand on his own and said it was fair. This was the single best opening on the call and it was not taken — the rep replied 'Good for him' and moved on. Two minutes later he cut the price in half, which directly contradicted the frame the prospect had just handed him.

anchors.raw: probably a month and a half ago, bought some kettlebells, and I've been doing more and more workouts at home, trying to keep them, you know, 30 minutes or less, which I've loved… I just like pick random workouts from random people.
anchors.competitor: Free Instagram content, including Trevor's own
anchors.note: The second prospect in this batch already running successfully on the company's free content. He found Trevor the night before the call by clicking 'the first guy that I clicked on last night that had a link to training and not just a PDF to download'. The free tier is doing the demand generation and simultaneously supplying a workable substitute, which is now a repeated pattern rather than an isolated one.

unmet_demand.want: A lower-priced way into the ecosystem. Asked for explicitly and specifically: 'Are there other trainers or anything that don't command such a high price point? Are there other people on his team?'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He was told none exists — 'No, all the stuff we do is one-on-one with Trevor, so we don't have it, we don't have anybody else's' — when Primal University exists at roughly $2,000 annually and is, by the manager's own description, exactly where prospects like this are routed: 'those are usually the guys we send to Primal U.' The rep proposed selling him precisely that the following day. This is not a product gap at all, it is a prospect asking for a product that exists and being told it does not.

unmet_demand.want: Proof that the kettlebell programming would actually support endurance performance. He named this as his first must-have and the reason he would not just download a PDF: 'I want to know that the exercises that I'm doing are supporting my endurance goals as a whole... I want to know that they're additive to my overall goals.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Asserted, never evidenced. 'So we're getting the strength. It's directly helping the endurance things' was the whole of it. No mechanism, no example of an endurance athlete client, nothing about how a programme is periodised around a 12-mile swim in August or a ski descent in June, both of which he had named. For a prospect who plans four months out for a mountain, this was the specific proof that would have closed him and it was never offered.

unmet_demand.want: Programming that respects bilateral shoulder instability. He set his own hard limits: no overhead barbell, no full-extension pull-ups, light snatches only.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Answered with a cure claim rather than an accommodation plan — that shoulder problems are 'just completely gone' after the programme because 'kettlebells strengthen around those injuries so well'. Nothing about assessment, load management, movement substitution or whether a clinician should be involved. Marked unvalidated rather than a gap because the programme may well adapt properly; the call gives no basis to judge, and the claim made instead is the subject of a critical integrity flag.

unmet_demand.want: Low-touch, asynchronous delivery. Stated plainly as a preference: 'I don't care about, like, you know, face-to-face calls. If it's asynchronous, it's really good.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The programme is already largely asynchronous — app-delivered workouts, video form review, weekly written check-ins, text access — which is close to exactly what he asked for. Nobody framed it that way. The accountability pillar was pitched around calls, community and coaching contact, and the one live element, the onboarding call with Trevor, was foregrounded. A stated preference that the product already satisfies was left looking like a mismatch.

unmet_demand.want: A training structure that survives the arrival of a first child in four months — his actual stated reason for being on the call: 'I want the confidence that I have good routines that I can carry forward into that... I may not have time to train eight, ten hours a week when we have a kid.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Partially served and then mishandled. The rep did connect the programme to the deadline, but at the close he converted the baby from a reason into a pressure device — 'your baby's born. And now we're looking at nine months... it's taken away directly from time with your girl, dude.' The legitimate version of this argument, that a 20-minute customised routine is precisely what survives a newborn, was available all call and was largely left unmade in favour of urgency.
